1:
The date is given with unusual precision and everyone stops on it. Gill and Wesley reckon it from the captivity of Jehoiachin, which coincided with the reign of Zedekiah, so that the ninth year may be named either way. Ellicott confirms the identification, noting that the same date appears in three other places and that it was afterwards kept by the Jews as a fast; it was doubtless the day on which the investment of the city was completed. Keil and Delitzsch say the same and specify the manner, that the king blockaded the city by throwing up a rampart. Clarke goes further than any of them and puts a day of the week and a year of the world to it.

What matters is that the news travelled no ordinary way. Henry points out the distance, many days journey from Jerusalem to Babylon, and supposes the last intelligence the exiles had was that the campaign would open against Rabbath of the children of Ammon; yet the prophet could say that on this very day the city was invested and the Chaldean army sat down before it. As all times, so all places, even the most remote, are present with God and under his view. Ellicott refuses the natural explanation outright: the supposition that the reference is to some point on the march from which the king advanced, and that tidings reached the prophet in the ordinary way, is quite inconsistent with the verse, since he means with especial emphasis that he was informed of what was happening at Jerusalem on the day it happened. Ellicott also corrects the English, preferring has fallen upon to has set himself against.

The order to write it down has a purpose. Henry has the prophet enter it in his book as a memorandum, so that when the report proved punctually true, as the exiles would find in a little time by the public intelligence, it would confirm his commission; being right in his news, he might be inferred right in his predictions, since he owed both to the same correspondence with heaven. Keil and Delitzsch say the same of both audiences at once, that the exiles and the besieged alike might learn from the time and from the result that the destruction of the city was not to be ascribed to chance. Gill takes the naming of the day literally as the day of the week as well as of the month, remarking that the Jews had no other names for their days than the numbers. Clarke sets out the shape of the whole chapter: the siege announced, its fate described under a very apt similitude, then the prophet forbidden to mourn for his wife as a sign that the sufferings would surpass all expression of grief and that private sorrow, however tender its object, ought to be absorbed in the public calamity.
3:
Ellicott settles two things. What follows was not a symbolical action but a parable spoken, although the language is that of action; and the pot is the cauldron, the word carrying the definite article because it refers back to an earlier chapter in which the people themselves had called their city a cauldron. So let it be, the word now says: set that city on the fire of my judgment, and gather into it for destruction the people who boasted of it as their security. Gill notes that the house is called rebellious not so much for rebelling against the king of Babylon as against God.

Clarke supplies a key to the figure: the pot is Jerusalem, the flesh its inhabitants, the good pieces the king and his family, the bones the soldiers, and the setting on of the pot the beginning of the siege; he remarks that the image was familiar to a priest, and that an earlier prophet had used a boiling pot for the same siege. Wesley reads the good pieces as the wealthiest who fled their country houses for the city and the most warlike who came to defend it. Ellicott disagrees with both on one point: the mention of the good piece and the choice bones is not meant to designate any particular class, but only to emphasise that all, even the best, are included.

The bones give trouble. Ellicott will not force the sense: the word for burn is really a noun meaning a heap, and many supply a verb to make it a heap of wood for burning the bones, while most ancient versions give the sense of the text; since bones with the fat still in them can be used for fuel, he translates literally, heap the bones under it, leaving the ambiguity of the original as to whether they are burned on the fuel or used as it. Wesley takes them differently, as the bones of the innocents murdered in the city, whose blood cries for vengeance and will maintain the fire.

The rust and the blood carry the charge. Ellicott notes that the word rendered scum occurs five times here and nowhere else, and that interpreters agree with the old Greek version in giving rust: not only are the inhabitants wicked, but the wickedness is so great that the city itself is corroded, and must be brought out piece by piece with no lot falling to discriminate, all previous judgments having been partial and this one complete. On the blood upon the rock, Clarke and Ellicott agree that the law required blood to be poured on the ground and covered with dust, and that the city had laid the blood of her victims on bare rock uncovered, glorying in her shame. Ellicott observes that what is charged on the city in one verse is claimed by God in the next, and finds no inconsistency, since she gloried in her crimes and God made them conspicuous as the cause of her punishment.

At the end the cauldron is set empty on the coals. Ellicott keeps the figure strict: after the inhabitants have passed under judgment the city itself is purged by fire, and the thought is not of heat removing rust but of the legal purifying of defiled metal vessels, a symbolic purification which here meant the actual destruction of the city. He corrects two words as well, the wearying with lies being rather that the labour is in vain, and the lewdness rather an abomination. Clarke presses the same word as denoting the worst impurities together with the settled purpose to commit them, so that these were not accidental sins but abominations by design.
15:
Henry marks the place: these verses conclude the prophecies of the destruction of the city, after which the prophet said no more about it until he heard of its fall almost three years later. Having shown that the trouble could not be prevented, he now assures them they will not even have the ease of weeping for it. The sign cost the prophet dear, and Henry thinks it the more shameful that people so expensively addressed were not moved. He allows himself three observations on the marriage: that a married state agrees well with the prophetic office, being honourable in all and therefore not sinful in ministers; that much of the comfort of human life lies in agreeable relations, and that a prudent and tender companion who shared his griefs and cares must have been a happiness in his captivity; and that those in that relation must be to each other not only a covering of the eyes, restraining wandering looks, but a desire of the eyes. Wesley adds the general lesson, that we do not know how soon the desire of our eyes may be removed, death being a stroke from which the most pious and useful are not exempt.

Clarke reads the prohibition as a statement about the depth of the grief rather than only a sign: the stroke was to be above all grief, so great as to prevent the relief of tears. He supports it twice over, with the old maxim that light cares speak while heavier ones are silent, and with a passage of a Greek novelist to the effect that in moderate misfortunes tears flow freely, but in overwhelming ones they fly away and betray the eyes. Gill notes that the opening word is meant to raise the attention of the prophet, something strange and affecting being about to be said.

The forbidden customs are itemised. Clarke lists them: as a priest he could make no public mourning; the tire of the head may be the priestly bonnet or a black veil; walking barefoot was a sign of grief; mourners covered the face from the nose to the chin; and the bread of men is the bread of mourners, probably the funeral banquet. Ellicott doubts the priestly dress, since the peculiar garments were worn only on duty within the tabernacle and are unlikely to have been used in captivity, and he adds the more important point that priests were expressly allowed to mourn for their nearest relations, so that the prophet is here made an exception. He collects the ordinary signs from elsewhere, covering the head, sprinkling dust on it, going barefoot and covering the lower part of the face, all now forbidden; and he explains the bread of men as bread furnished by others, it being customary for friends and neighbours to send food to a house of mourning, a custom out of which funeral feasts appear later to have grown. Wesley says the tire is to be bound as usual, so that he does not go bare-headed like a mourner.

Ellicott reconstructs the day. What the prophet spoke to the people in the morning was the parable of the cauldron; shortly after, the warning about his wife came to him; she died that evening; and on the following morning his strange conduct was observed, so that their curiosity was awakened and they came to ask what it meant. Gill says he told them beforehand what he had been ordered to do, so that when it came to pass they might have a further proof that he was a true prophet. Clarke states the typology plainly, that the wife was a type of the city, exceedingly dear to him, and her death represented its destruction, as the following verses call the temple the desire of his eyes in the same words used of her.
19:
Gill allows two motives for the question. The people may have asked seriously, since they had reason to think it was not want of affection in the prophet that made him behave so, and there must be some hidden meaning they would be glad to learn; or they may have asked in derision, mocking his conduct and despising what he meant to teach by it. Clarke simply notes that the following verses explain and apply the whole. The answer names the sanctuary, and Ellicott sharpens what profaning it means: not merely its destruction but the manner of it, the Gentiles being allowed into its most sacred precincts and carrying off its vessels and treasures in triumph. The last hope of the people lay in the confidence that God would protect it, and he tells them that he will profane it himself. Wesley makes the parallel exact, that the sanctuary was as much their desire as the wife was the desire of the prophet.

What was required of him is then required of them. Gill reads the tires on their heads and the shoes on their feet as the dress of people travelling, as they would be when carried into a foreign country; Wesley says they will be where they may not use their own customs. Ellicott explains the pining: in the tumult and distress of the judgment there would be no opportunity for the outward display of grief, so that it must press on them the more inwardly, and he connects the phrase with an older threatening that they should pine away in their iniquity in the land of their enemies, noting that the preposition is the same in both places. Wesley puts it that they shall languish with secret sorrow where they dare not show it openly.

The chapter ends by setting a term to the silence of the prophet. Keil and Delitzsch recall the standing rule under which he lived, that he was to speak to the people only when the Lord gave him a word for them and to remain dumb at other times. Ellicott measures the interval: from the investment of the city until he heard of its fall, almost two years, he gave no prophecy to Israel, having abundantly foretold the result and now awaiting the issue in silence, though he recorded during that time a considerable number of prophecies against foreign nations. Ellicott also marks the structural break, that one great division of the book closes here, that the collection which follows is arranged by nation rather than chronologically, and that after the news of the fall reached him the tone of the prophet changes markedly and becomes far more consolatory. Clarke confirms that one did in fact escape and bring the news, so that the agreement of the prediction with the event proved the earlier information came from the Lord; and he observes that the prophet was not only a foreteller but himself a sign, shadowing out the events in his own person and family. Wesley counts the silence at eighteen months.
